concepts.def: A computer design in which instructions and data are stored together in the same main memory and share the same buses to the processor.
A register holding the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched, incremented automatically during each fetch-decode-execute cycle.
A register holding the address of the memory location currently being read from or written to during a memory access.
A register that temporarily holds the data or instruction just read from memory, or about to be written to memory.
Sets of parallel wires connecting processor and memory: the address bus carries addresses, the data bus carries data, and the control bus carries control signals.
The repeating cycle in which the processor fetches an instruction from memory, decodes what it means, then executes the required operation.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Fundamentals Of Computer Organisation & Architecture — a core area of A-Level Computer Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Fundamentals Of Computer Organisation & Architecture brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Fundamentals Of Computer Organisation & Architecture.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which register holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched?
options: Memory buffer register
Accumulator
Program counter
Current instruction register

mcqs.q: During the fetch stage, the address held in the program counter is copied to the:
options: Accumulator
Memory address register
Status register
Arithmetic logic unit

mcqs.q: Which bus carries memory addresses from the processor to main memory?
options: Data bus
Control bus
Universal serial bus
Address bus

mcqs.q: A defining feature of the von Neumann architecture is that:
options: Instructions and data are stored in the same memory and share the same buses
Instructions and data are kept in physically separate memories
No registers are used by the processor
Programs cannot be changed once loaded

mcqs.q: Does the program counter hold the current instruction?
options: No - the program counter holds the ADDRESS of the next instruction; the current instruction itself sits in the current instruction register after being fetched.
Yes - the program counter counts how many programs are installed.
Yes - doubling the GHz exactly doubles every program's speed.
Yes - the program counter stores the instruction being executed.

mcqs.q: Does a higher clock speed always mean a faster computer?
options: Yes - clock speed is the only factor that determines performance.
Yes - the program counter counts how many programs are installed.
Yes - doubling the GHz exactly doubles every program's speed.
No - performance also depends on cores, cache size, memory speed and how much work each cycle achieves, so a lower-clocked CPU can outperform a higher-clocked one.

mcqs.q: In the von Neumann architecture, are instructions and data stored in separate memories?
options: Yes - von Neumann machines keep programs and data physically apart.
Yes - instructions are stored only inside the ALU.
Yes - doubling the GHz exactly doubles every program's speed.
No - they share one main memory and one set of buses; the Harvard architecture is the design that separates instruction and data memory.

sequence.term: PC holds the next instruction's address
sequence.def: The program counter says where in memory to look
It travels via the address and data buses into the CPU
The current instruction register holds it for decoding
The ALU and registers carry out the operation
The PC has moved on; the next fetch begins
